messages.author: 39971e2c19b8ec70
messages.subject: Prior for spatial length-scale?
parts:
Hello,

what is the default prior for spatial length-scale in spatial (e.g.
SPDE) models?

I've been looking in INLA documentation but didn't find it.

I am especially interested if there is any Penalized Complexity prior
for this parameter, or not.

Thanks,

Tomas

messages.author: afb003e064114795
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Prior for spatial length-scale?
parts:
For pc-prior for SPDE matern models, see
?inla.spde.pcmatern
By design, that one doesn’t have any default parameters for the prior.
The documentation explains the parameters.

The inla.spde.matern models use a log-gaussian prior for tau and kappa, with prior mean zero. I recommend agains using the default parameters (that feature is only still there for backwards compatibility). Instead, see the approach in the journal of statistical software, Lindgren&Rue “Bayesian Spatial Modelling with R-INLA”.
You can find this on r-inla.org, under
“Examples and tutorials”-“Tutorials”-“Read this first!”

Finn

parts:
Dear Finn,

thanks for answer! I've been looking into it more deeply and have some
more questions:

1) You recommended against something and referred to Lindgren & Rue
... which is not referring to the pcmatern prior. I just want to make
sure I understand this correctly - so is it recommended to use the
prior described in Fuglstad 2019 (see screenshot) - i.e. the
inla.spde2.pcmatern? I guess the answer is yes, I just want to clear
possible confusions :)

2) In my current application (my own code, not using INLA), I am using
Matern with v = 3/2, which has nice simplification and is easy to
compute. When I look into INLA, maximum alpha I can use is 2, and d=2,
which means that maximum v possible (and the default value) in INLA is
v = alpha - d/2 = 1? Is that correct?

So you most of the times use v = 1? Up to now I've seen papers to use
Matern with v = 3/2; do you have any comparison with that?

3) The definition of the joint PC prior (see the screenshot) doesn't
seem to depend on the parameter v, am I right? So do you think it
could be used even with the value of v = 3/2, if I want to keep my old
function?

Thanks!

Tomas

messages.author: afb003e064114795
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Prior for spatial length-scale?
parts:
On Mon, 20 Apr 2020 at 13:20, Tomas T. <tomas.t...@gmail.com> wrote:
> 1) You recommended against something and referred to Lindgren & Rue
> ... which is not referring to the pcmatern prior. I just want to make
> sure I understand this correctly - so is it recommended to use the
> prior described in Fuglstad 2019 (see screenshot) - i.e. the
> inla.spde2.pcmatern? I guess the answer is yes, I just want to clear
> possible confusions :)

Worst: inla.spde2.matern with default parameters
Better: inla.spde2.matern with more sensible parameters, as in Lindgren&Rue.
Best: inla.spde2.pcmatern with sensibly chosen parameters, as in Fuglstad 2019

> 2) In my current application (my own code, not using INLA), I am using
> Matern with v = 3/2, which has nice simplification and is easy to
> compute. When I look into INLA, maximum alpha I can use is 2, and d=2,
> which means that maximum v possible (and the default value) in INLA is
> v = alpha - d/2 = 1? Is that correct?

In d=2, nu=3/2 isn't a Markov field, so needs other approximations,
which we've only directly implemented
up to alpha=2 (0 < nu <=1).
You can use the equations in the Authors' response to the 2011
Lindgren et al SPDE/GRMF to
implement the fractional models for higher alpha values as an rgeneric model.
But the higher nu values quickly become hard to distinguish from each other.
Whether the difference between nu = 1 and nu = 3/2 is important
depends on your problem.
Much spatial statistics uses nu = 1/2 (which is Markov in 1D and 3D
but not in 2D), but I'd
argue that that's largely due to convenience, just as your 3/2 case.

> So you most of the times use v = 1? Up to now I've seen papers to use
> Matern with v = 3/2; do you have any comparison with that?

> 3) The definition of the joint PC prior (see the screenshot) doesn't
> seem to depend on the parameter v, am I right? So do you think it
> could be used even with the value of v = 3/2, if I want to keep my old
> function?

I don't recall the specifics, but it may be applicable, yes. I do
think there's a dimension dependence,
and the range and variance are linked to nu, so there may be hidden
dependencies.
Would need to check the details of the Fuglstad paper.

Finn
